entry: Colorless organic compound (systematic name ethanal, CH₃CH=O) and one of the most important [[Aldehyde|aldehydes]]. It occurs naturally in coffee, bread and ripe fruit, and is formed when the liver enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase partly oxidizes [[Ethanol|ethanol]], contributing to hangover after drinking. Global production was about 438,000 tonnes in 2013, mainly by the oxidation of ethylene. Human studies have not established a cause-and-effect link with cancer, although the International Agency for Research on Cancer has listed it as a carcinogen.

Colorless, acidic organic compound (systematic name ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH) and the active component of [[Vinegar|vinegar]]. It is the second simplest [[Carboxylic acid|carboxylic acid]], after [[Formic acid|formic acid]]. Its main uses are the production of cellulose acetate for photographic film, polyvinyl acetate for wood glue, and synthetic fibers and fabrics. In the food industry it is controlled as the additive E260 and used as an acidity regulator and condiment. In biochemistry the acetyl group derived from it is fundamental to all forms of life; bound to coenzyme A, it is central to the metabolism of carbohydrates and fats. Global demand was about 17.88 million metric tonnes a year as of 2023, and most acetic acid is made by the carbonylation of [[Methanol|methanol]]. Concentrated acetic acid is corrosive and flammable.

Colorless, highly volatile and flammable organic compound (2-propanone, (CH₃)₂CO), the simplest [[Ketone|ketone]]. It is miscible with water and is an important solvent in industry, households and laboratories, used in products such as nail polish remover and paint thinner. About 6.7 million tonnes were produced worldwide in 2010, mainly for making methyl methacrylate and bisphenol A, precursors to widely used plastics. About 83% of acetone is produced by the cumene process, in which benzene is alkylated with propylene and the resulting cumene is oxidized to give acetone and phenol. Small amounts occur naturally in blood and urine, and people with diabetic ketoacidosis produce larger amounts. Ketogenic diets that raise blood ketone bodies, including acetone, are used to suppress seizures in children with treatment-resistant [[Epilepsy|epilepsy]].

Colorless gas (systematic name ethyne, C₂H₂, HC≡CH), the simplest [[Alkyne|alkyne]] and a widely used fuel and chemical building block. Its carbon–carbon triple bond makes it highly endothermic, and it is unstable in pure form, so it is usually handled as a solution. Since the 1950s it has mainly been made by the partial combustion of methane in the U.S. and much of the European Union. It is used in oxyacetylene welding and cutting of metals, with a flame reaching up to 3,300°C in oxygen.

Hero of the Trojan War in Greek mythology, the central character of Homer's *Iliad*. He was regarded as the greatest of the Greek warriors, the son of the Nereid Thetis and Peleus, king of Phthia, and was educated by the centaur Chiron. In the *Iliad* he commands the Myrmidons, and his most notable feat is the slaying of the Trojan prince Hector outside the gates of Troy. The *Iliad* does not describe his death, but other sources say he was killed near the end of the war by Paris, who shot him with an arrow. Later legend, first recorded in Statius's unfinished epic *Achilleid* in the first century AD, held that he was invulnerable except in one heel, which Thetis held when she dipped him in the river Styx. The phrase Achilles' heel now denotes a point of weakness, and the Achilles tendon is named after him.

Chemical reaction between an acid and a base, used in titration to determine pH. Several theoretical frameworks describe these reactions. The concept was first proposed in 1754 by Guillaume-François Rouelle, who introduced the word base into chemistry. Antoine Lavoisier defined acids by their oxygen content around 1776, a view that Humphry Davy undermined in 1810 by showing that hydrogen sulfide and the hydrohalic acids contain no oxygen. Justus von Liebig defined acids in 1838 as hydrogen-containing compounds whose hydrogen can be replaced by a metal. The Arrhenius definition describes an acid as a substance that increases the concentration of hydrogen ions in aqueous solution, and a base as one that increases hydroxide ions; it led to Svante Arrhenius's Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1903. The Lewis model is the broadest, with the Brønsted–Lowry theory a subset of it.

Precipitation that is unusually acidic, with a pH below 5. Clean rain has a pH between 5 and 7 because of dissolved carbon dioxide. Acid rain is caused mainly by emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which react with water in the atmosphere to form sulfuric and nitric acids. It harms forests, freshwaters, soils and aquatic life, and strips soils of nutrients such as calcium and magnesium. It also peels paint, corrodes steel and weathers stone buildings and statues. Robert Angus Smith showed the link to air pollution in Manchester, England, in 1852 and coined the term in 1872. Since the 1970s, governments in Europe and North America have reduced sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions through air-quality laws such as the U.S. Clean Air Act.

Common long-term skin condition in which dead skin cells and sebum clog hair follicles, producing blackheads, whiteheads, pimples and possible scarring. It mainly affects the face, upper chest and back, where oil glands are most numerous. Susceptibility is primarily genetic in about 80% of cases. In both sexes, androgens increase sebum production, and the bacterium *Cutibacterium acnes* contributes to the condition. Treatments include benzoyl peroxide, azelaic acid and salicylic acid applied to the skin, [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]], retinoids and some birth control pills. Isotretinoin is reserved for severe acne because of its greater potential side effects. In 2015 acne affected about 633 million people worldwide. It affects an estimated 80–90% of teenagers in the Western world, and persists into the twenties and thirties in nearly half of those affected.

Mountain in the Principal Cordillera of the [[Andes]] in Mendoza Province, Argentina. With a summit elevation of 6,967.15 m (22,858 ft), it is the highest mountain outside Asia and one of the Seven Summits, the highest peaks on each continent. It was formed by the subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South American Plate and was an active stratovolcano until the [[Miocene]], about 8 to 10 million years ago, when tectonic shifts halted volcanism. The first recorded ascent was made on January 14, 1897, by the Swiss guide Matthias Zurbriggen, on a British expedition led by Edward FitzGerald. The normal route from the north is technically straightforward, but at an altitude where pressure is about 40% of sea level, altitude sickness affects most climbers. About three deaths a year are recorded, and summit success rates are estimated at 30–40%.

Branch of continuum mechanics that studies mechanical waves in gases, liquids and solids, including vibration, sound, ultrasound and infrasound. Its specialists are called acousticians. The field is applied in almost every part of modern society, most obviously in audio and noise-control industries, and also in music, medicine, architecture, industrial production and warfare. In the 6th century BCE, [[Pythagoras]] is reputed to have found that musical tones are harmonious when string lengths are simple whole-number ratios. [[Aristotle]] understood that sound consists of compressions and rarefactions of air. Around 20 BCE the Roman architect [[Vitruvius]] wrote a treatise on the acoustic properties of theaters. Modern applications include [[Sonar|sonar]], ultrasound imaging and the design of concert halls.

Unit of land area in the British imperial and United States customary systems. It is traditionally defined as one chain by one furlong (66 by 660 feet), which equals 43,560 square feet, 4,840 square yards, one 640th of a square mile, and about 4,047 square meters, or roughly 40% of a [[Hectare|hectare]]. In the Middle Ages an acre was conceived as the land one man with a team of eight oxen could plow in a day. The acre remains a statute measure in the United States, where the international and survey acres differ by only four parts per million. The United Kingdom ceased to use it as a statute measure in 2010, and Australia, New Zealand and South Africa dropped it decades earlier. A square acre measures about 208 feet 9 inches on a side.

Performance of human feats of balance, agility and motor coordination. Acrobatic skills are used in performing arts, sporting events and martial arts, most often in acro dance, circus, gymnastics and freerunning, and to a lesser extent in ballet, slacklining and diving. Acrobatic performers are shown in Egyptian tombs from around 2000 BCE, and Minoan frescoes from Knossos (c. 1500 BCE) depict bull-leaping. Acrobatics was part of military training in ancient Greece and theatrical entertainment in Rome, and in China it was combined with juggling and tightrope walking. By the 18th and 19th centuries it was a cornerstone of the circus, and Jules Léotard introduced the flying trapeze in 1859. Acrobatic gymnastics emerged in the Soviet Union in the 1930s and became a competitive sport under the International Gymnastics Federation.

Disorder of excess growth in parts of the body, caused by excess growth hormone after the growth plates have closed. The first symptom is typically enlarged hands and feet, and the forehead, jaw and nose may also enlarge. Joint pain, thickened skin, a deepened voice, headaches and vision problems may follow. Complications include type 2 diabetes, sleep apnea and high blood pressure.

Ancient citadel on a rocky outcrop above the city of Athens, Greece, with the remains of several major buildings, most famously the [[Parthenon]]. The word acropolis means highest point of the city. The hill was inhabited as early as the 4th millennium BC. In the fifth century BC [[Pericles]] coordinated the construction of the buildings that survive, including the Parthenon, the Propylaea, the Erechtheion and the Temple of Athena Nike. The complex was dedicated to [[Athena]], Athens's patron goddess. In 1687 the Parthenon and other buildings were badly damaged in a Venetian siege, when gunpowder stored by the Turkish rulers exploded after a Venetian bombardment. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, designated in 1987.

Activity in which a story is told through an [[Actor|actor's]] enactment of a character in theater, television, film, radio or any other mimetic medium. It draws on imagination, emotional range, physical expressivity, vocal projection, clarity of speech and the ability to interpret drama, and may require dialects, accents, improvisation and stage combat. The vast majority of professional actors undergo extensive training. Western writing on acting began as part of rhetoric in ancient Greece, where the performer was called *hupokritēs*. The first known individual actor, Thespis of Icaria, is credited with stepping out from the chorus around 534 BCE. [[Konstantin Stanislavski]]'s system, developed in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, emphasizes psychological depth and emotional memory, and it inspired American Method acting.

Series of metallic chemical elements with atomic numbers 89 to 102, from [[Actinium|actinium]] through nobelium. The 14 elements of the 5f series are the core of the group, and lawrencium (103) is also generally included, although it belongs to the 6d transition series. All actinides are radioactive. Only thorium and uranium occur on Earth in substantial quantities, because of their long half-lives, while plutonium is produced synthetically. Uranium and plutonium are critical elements of [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapons]], and uranium and thorium have been used in [[Nuclear reactor|nuclear reactors]]. Americium is used in the ionization chambers of most modern smoke detectors. Actinium through nobelium are f-block elements, and actinide valence is much more variable than that of the lanthanides.

Radioactive chemical element (symbol Ac, atomic number 89), the first of the [[Actinide|actinides]]. It is a soft, silvery-white metal that reacts rapidly with oxygen and moisture, forming a white oxide coating. It occurs only in traces in uranium and thorium ores, where its isotope actinium-227 decays with a half-life of 21.772 years. Chemically it resembles lanthanum, so it is impractical to separate from ore; milligram amounts are instead made by neutron irradiation of radium-226 in a nuclear reactor. Owing to its scarcity, high price and radioactivity, actinium has no significant industrial use. Its applications include a neutron source and an agent for radiation therapy.

Class of bony fishes, also called ray-finned fishes. The class makes up nearly 99% of the more than 30,000 living fish species and more than half of all living vertebrates. Most are teleosts. Their fins are light webs of skin supported by bony rays called lepidotrichia, unlike the fleshy fins of the sister clade [[Sarcopterygii]]. They live in freshwater, brackish and marine environments from the deep sea to mountain streams. Living species range from the Paedocypris, at 8 mm, to the giant sunfish, at 2,700 kg, and the giant oarfish, at about 8 m. The extinct Leedsichthys of the Jurassic is the largest known ray-finned fish, estimated at 16.5 m.

Poseable character figure, most commonly made of plastic, based on characters from film, comic books, television, video games or sports. The term was coined by Hasbro in 1964 to market G.I. Joe to boys, while competitors called similar offerings boys' dolls. A 2005 study in Sweden found that action figures displaying traditional masculine traits primarily target boys. Tie-ins with franchises such as [[Star Wars]], beginning in 1978, fueled the genre's popularity in the late 1970s and 1980s. Adult collectors now form a large share of the market, which generated about US$8.59 billion in revenue as of 2025. Action figures are also often used in stop-motion animation.

Film genre that predominantly features chase sequences, fights, shootouts, explosions and stunt work. Scholars have debated its definition since the 1980s. David Bordwell has argued that action films favor spectacle over storytelling, while Geoff King holds that spectacle can be attuned to the story. The contemporary form emerged with New Hollywood and the anti-heroes of American films of the late 1960s and 1970s, drawing on war films, crime films and Westerns. It was later influenced by Hong Kong action cinema and computer-generated imagery. Action films are often hybrids with comedies, science fiction films and horror films. The genre is popular with audiences but often derided for favoring spectacle over narrative.

Compact region at a galaxy's center with abnormally high luminosity. An active galactic nucleus (AGN) emits significant energy across the electromagnetic spectrum, in radio, microwave, infrared, optical, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma-ray wavebands. This non-stellar radiation is theorized to result from the accretion of matter by a [[Supermassive black hole|supermassive black hole]] at the galaxy's center. AGN are the most luminous persistent sources of electromagnetic radiation in the universe. Their observed characteristics depend on the black hole's mass, the rate of gas accretion, the orientation of the accretion disk, dust obscuration and the presence of jets. The most powerful are classified as [[Quasar|quasars]]. A [[Blazar|blazar]] is an AGN with a jet pointed toward Earth. The central black hole of the [[Milky Way]] is not active but is believed to have been active about 8 billion years ago.

Movement of molecules or ions across a cell membrane from lower to higher concentration, against the concentration gradient and using cellular energy. Primary active transport uses [[Adenosine triphosphate|adenosine triphosphate]] (ATP), while secondary active transport uses an electrochemical gradient. Passive transport, by contrast, moves substances down their gradient without energy. Active transport is essential for nutrient uptake, hormone secretion and impulse transmission. The sodium–potassium pump uses ATP to move sodium ions out of the cell and potassium ions in, maintaining gradients essential for cell function. Defects in transport underlie disorders such as cystic fibrosis, caused by a malfunctioning [[Chloride|chloride]] channel, and diabetes, which results from defective glucose transport into cells.

Efforts to promote, impede, direct or intervene in social, political, economic or environmental reform toward a perceived common good. Forms range from writing letters and petitioning elected officials to contributing to [[Political campaign|political campaigns]], boycotts, rallies, street marches, strikes, sit-ins and hunger strikes. Activism becomes a [[Social movement|social movement]] when collective action is purposeful, organized and sustained over time. Activists have long used pamphlets and books to persuade readers. Research on online activism finds that left-wing and right-wing activists often use different tactics: hashtag activism and offline protest are more common on the left, while working with partisan media is more common on the right in the United States. Separating activism from [[Terrorism|terrorism]] can be difficult.

Person who portrays a character in a production, in the flesh on the stage or in film, radio and television. The term is masculine or gender-neutral; actress is the feminine form. The Greek term *hupokritēs* meant one who answers. In ancient Greece and the medieval world, and in England at the time of [[William Shakespeare]], only men could become actors, and women's roles were played by men or boys. Ancient Rome allowed female performers, but few were given speaking parts. The [[Commedia dell'arte]] of Italy admitted professional women early on; Lucrezia Di Siena, named on a contract dated October 10, 1564, is the first Italian actress known by name. Women began to appear on the English stage after the Restoration of 1660.

Form of alternative medicine, a component of traditional Chinese medicine, in which thin needles are inserted into the body. It is most often used for pain relief, though practitioners say it can treat a wide range of other conditions. Scientific investigation has found no histological or physiological evidence for the qi, meridians or acupuncture points on which its traditional theories rest. Trials and systematic reviews generally find no good evidence of benefit, and sham acupuncture often produces similar results, although some reviews report short-term pain relief compared with no treatment. It is generally safe when practitioners use clean, single-use needles; the most frequently reported adverse events are pneumothorax and infections. Acupuncture is believed to have originated around 100 BC in China and spread to Korea in the 6th century AD, then to Japan and Europe.
